My manager forwarded me a screenshot of my own benchmark chart with one line attached: explain why this is not already in production.
That message sat in my inbox for a full day before I answered it, because the honest answer made me look like the person who wasted three weeks proving a point nobody asked me to prove.
Here is the setup. Our checkout service handles about one million requests a day during sale events. Someone on the team suggested we test whether Rust could beat our existing stack on raw throughput. It could.
It won by a wide margin, and I got the kind of applause in the team channel that makes you want to keep going. That applause is the villain of this story, not Rust itself.
Every conference talk, every glowing blog post about rewriting some service in Rust and watching latency drop, trains developers to treat a fast chart as a finished decision.
It is not a finished decision. It is the first slide of a much longer argument.
The Benchmark Everyone Screenshots
We built a stripped down version of our order validation endpoint and ran the same logic in three languages, same hardware, same limits.
